source.title: Enhancing Sample Selection Against Label Noise by Cutting Mislabeled Easy Examples
source.authors: Su-Qin Yuan; Lei Feng; Bo Han; Tong-Liang Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study tests learning dynamics under instance-dependent label noise and reports that some mislabeled samples are learned early and harm generalization more than later-learned mislabeled samples. This refines the broad real-label-first account in V6; it does not test fitting completely random labels.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own results on when mislabeled examples are learned and on their effects on model performance. Competitor comparisons and cited prior results are not extracted as rows. Figure-only learning-speed and test-accuracy curves are represented only where the text describes their direction.
record.test_reason: The study reports early learning of some instance-dependent mislabeled examples, qualifying V6's real-label-first account. Its generalization, feature-distance and influence measurements do not themselves measure learning order.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors identify early-learned mislabeled examples as disproportionately harmful and propose later-stage recalibration to remove them. They describe the explanation of this harm as primarily observational.
record.recipe_differences: Studies learning order and comparative harm of instance-dependent mislabeled examples, using sample-group training, feature-space measurements, and influence functions; does not use the original random-label intervention.

fits_no_version.finding: Earlier-learned mislabeled groups reduce test accuracy more than later-learned groups.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mislabeled examples differ in generalization harm according to their learning order.

fits_no_version.finding: MEEs have median incorrect-to-true class distance ratio 0.830 versus 3.923 for other mislabeled examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early-learned mislabeled examples more often resemble their incorrect classes in early feature representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean harmful influence is 4.96 for early-learned versus 3.01 for late-learned mislabeled examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early-learned mislabeled examples have greater estimated harmful influence on clean validation loss.

record.problems: The learning-order test uses instance-dependent label noise rather than completely random labels. Several learning-speed and generalization comparisons are shown as plots without exact values in the supplied text. The paper characterizes its explanation of MEE harm as primarily observational.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows beyond the reported CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 learning-order trends, CIFAR-10 feature-space ratios, and CIFAR-10 influence analysis. Figure 2/3/6/7 contain separate plotted groups, but exact group values are unavailable in the text; trends are recorded at the level explicitly described in prose.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance and unchanged training settings.
Relative time to fit true and random labels, and convergence slowing as corruption increases.
Training fit on shuffled, independently permuted or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily degrading test performance across a corruption sweep extending to fully random labels.
Effects of adding or removing explicit regularization on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
A direct population-level comparison of shared clean-pattern learning with noisy-label memorization; wholly random labels; whether clean-first learning remains the predominant tendency.

missing.what: Record the explicitly reported acquisition of incorrect assigned labels during early training, separately from downstream harm and feature distances. Learning in Section 2.1 requires agreement with the assigned label for two consecutive epochs; Figure 4's early-stage representation is at epoch 10. No clean-versus-noisy timing difference should be invented.
missing.locator: Sections 2.1–2.2, Equation 1, Figure 4 and Appendix E

missing.what: Figure 1(b) reports an ImageNet-1k learning-time histogram under 40% symmetric noise, an additional setting omitted from the record. Its caption uses first correct prediction, differing from Equation 1. The supplied text lacks readable histogram counts or clean/noisy timing comparisons, so its direction cannot be determined.

record.verdict_notes: States for rows linked to none describe their inability to establish a claim version, not whether their reported measurements occurred. No evidence establishes a wholesale reversal of V6.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training-time cost of fitting random versus true labels and convergence as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
A sweep from no corruption to all-random labels, perfect training fit across that sweep, and corresponding test-error trajectory.
Whether regularization or augmentation prevents fitting random labels or whether their removal changes true-label generalization.
The study tests the timing and relative harm of instance-dependent mislabeled examples, but not a direct comparison of learning shared real-label patterns with fitting completely random labels.

rows.subject: initial model on CIFAR-10
rows.operation_detail: Trained on noisy CIFAR-10, then divided mislabeled examples into five groups by learning time; separately trained new models on each group's combination with clean examples.

conditions.value: earliest-learned mislabeled examples combined with 30,000 clean examples; 4,000 mislabeled examples

rows.baseline: Datasets containing later-learned mislabeled groups; exact values figure only
rows.value: Models trained with the earliest-learned group exhibited significantly lower generalization performance; exact values figure only
rows.note: The paper states the trend across the five groups; exact plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Test accuracy measures the harm of previously ranked noisy groups, not clean-versus-noisy learning order. The measured subjects are newly trained models, not the initial model used to rank examples. The stated direction matches the text.

rows.subject: initial model on CIFAR-100
rows.operation_detail: Trained on noisy CIFAR-100, then divided mislabeled examples into five groups by learning time; separately trained new models on each group's combination with clean examples.

conditions.value: earliest-learned mislabeled examples combined with 30,000 clean examples; 4,000 mislabeled examples

rows.baseline: Datasets containing later-learned mislabeled groups; exact values figure only
rows.value: Similar findings are stated; models trained with earlier-learned mislabeled groups have lower generalization performance; exact values figure only
rows.note: The text says Figure 6 shows similar findings on CIFAR-100; exact plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Generalization harm does not establish V6's learning order. The measured subjects are newly trained models, not the initial ranking model. The CIFAR-100 trend is explicitly stated, but exact values are unavailable.

rows.subject: model pretrained on clean CIFAR-10 data
rows.stage_stated: pretrained on only the clean data
rows.operation_detail: After pretraining on clean data, trained on datasets combining clean examples with one of five groups of mislabeled examples.

conditions.value: mislabeled examples partitioned by initial model learning order

rows.baseline: Later-learned groups; exact epochs figure only
rows.value: The model learned the earliest-group examples much faster; exact epochs figure only
rows.note: The paper reports faster learning for the earliest group even when training starts from a model pretrained only on clean data.
rows.check: Earlier-ranked noisy examples are learned faster after clean pretraining, establishing heterogeneous noisy-label learning times. This does not directly compare clean-pattern acquisition with noisy-label memorization; clean learning precedes this experiment by design.

rows.subject: model trained on CIFAR-10
rows.operation_detail: Compared distances of early-learned mislabeled examples and remaining mislabeled examples to true-class and mislabeled-class centers in feature space.
rows.baseline: Non-MEEs: median 3.923; 5.4% closer to incorrect class
rows.note: This measures feature-space position, not direct fitting of random labels; included as evidence about early learning of mislabeled examples.
rows.check: The numbers are correctly extracted, but feature-space proximity does not measure learning order. Appendix E identifies the early measurement as epoch 10.

rows.subject: model trained on CIFAR-10
rows.operation_detail: Used influence functions to compare the impact of clean easy, mislabeled easy, and mislabeled hard examples on clean held-out validation loss.

conditions.value: first 4,000 mislabeled samples learned versus last 4,000 mislabeled samples learned

rows.measure: Mean influence score on clean held-out validation set
rows.note: The paper also reports median influence scores of 4.48 for MEEs and 3.26 for Mislabeled Hard Examples; and mean -2.22 for Clean Easy Examples.
rows.check: The influence scores are correctly extracted, but measure generalization harm rather than when clean and noisy labels are learned.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with instance-dependent label noise
relationships.reason: Sections 2.1–2.2 explicitly report mislabeled examples learned during early training; R3 and R4 show their relative ease persists after clean pretraining. This qualifies a blanket clean-first interpretation without establishing reversal of the overall tendency. The early-stage evidence requires the missing row.
relationships.display_finding: Some mislabeled examples were learned during early training and remained relatively easy after clean pretraining, qualifying a universal clean-first ordering.
